lessons.title: Say what you like, need and feel
lessons.summary: Say what you like, what you need and how you feel: “I like this city.” “I need a hat.” “I'm cold.”
lessons.topic: {{нра́вится|nrávitsa}} and {{нра́вятся|nrávyatsa}}; {{ну́жен|núzhen}}, {{нужна́|nuzhná}}, {{ну́жно|núzhno}}, {{нужны́|nuzhný}}; {{мне хо́лодно|mne khólodno}}, {{мне ску́чно|mne skúshno}}

goal.t: Мне о́чень нра́вится э́тот го́род.
goal.r: Mne óchen' nrávitsa étot górod.
goal.tr: I really like this city.

dialog.tr: Do you like Moscow?

dialog.t: Да, о́чень! Мне нра́вятся па́рки и метро́.
dialog.r: Da, óchen'! Mne nrávyatsa párki i metró.
dialog.tr: Yes, very much! I like the parks and the subway.
And the weather?
The weather, not so much. I'm cold!

dialog.t: Вам нужна́ ша́пка! Здесь ря́дом магази́н.
dialog.r: Vam nuzhná shápka! Zdes' ryádom magazín.
dialog.tr: You need a hat! There's a store nearby.
Thanks, I definitely need a hat.

blocks.p: **Like.** Russian turns “I like it” around: {{Мне нра́вится э́тот го́род.|Mne nrávitsa étot górod.}} is word for word “This city is pleasing to me”. The thing you like is the subject, in the nominative, and you are in the dative. So the verb agrees with the thing: {{нра́вится|nrávitsa}} for one thing, {{нра́вятся|nrávyatsa}} for several.

table: {{Мне нра́вится э́тот го́род.|Mne nrávitsa étot górod.}}

blocks.p: **{{нра́вится|nrávitsa}} or {{люблю́|lyublyú}}?** {{нра́вится|nrávitsa}} is for liking something, especially something new: a city, a dress, a movie. {{люблю́|lyublyú}} is stronger and lasts: things you love and always do. To say you liked something you saw or tried once, use the perfective past, which agrees with the thing: {{Мне понра́вился фильм.|Mne ponrávilsya fil'm.}} “I liked the movie.”, {{понра́вилась|ponrávilas'}} (feminine), {{понра́вилось|ponrávilos'}} (neuter), {{понра́вились|ponrávilis'}} (plural).

**Need.** {{Мне ну́жен…|Mne núzhen…}} “I need…” works the same way: the thing is the subject, and {{ну́жен|núzhen}} agrees with it: {{ну́жен|núzhen}}, {{нужна́|nuzhná}}, {{ну́жно|núzhno}}, {{нужны́|nuzhný}}. With a verb, it's {{ну́жно|núzhno}} or {{на́до|nádo}}, as you know: {{Мне ну́жно идти́.|Mne núzhno idtí.}}

**How you feel.** The same shape once more: the dative and a word in {{-о|-o}}. {{Мне хо́лодно.|Mne khólodno.}} “I'm cold.” {{Мне жа́рко.|Mne zhárko.}} “I'm hot.” {{Мне ску́чно.|Mne skúshno.}} “I'm bored.” {{Мне интере́сно.|Mne interésno.}} “I'm interested.” {{Мне пло́хо.|Mne plókho.}} “I feel sick.” {{Мне ве́село.|Mne véselo.}} “I'm having fun.”

ex.tr: Do you like my dress?
I don't like this music.
We really liked the restaurant.
Do you need a doctor?
I need new glasses.
He's bored at work.

mistakes.why: The thing you like is the subject; you are in the dative: {{мне|mne}}.
Several things: {{нра́вятся|nrávyatsa}}.
{{ну́жен|núzhen}} agrees with the thing: {{ша́пка|shápka}} is feminine, so {{нужна́|nuzhná}}.

practice.why: How you feel: {{мне|mne}} and {{хо́лодно|khólodno}}. {{Я холо́дный|Ya kholódnyy}} would mean you're a cold person!

lessons.title: Say what something is about
lessons.summary: Say what a book or a movie is about, what you're thinking about, and who you're talking about.
lessons.topic: {{о|o}} + the prepositional; {{обо мне|obo mne}}, {{о нём|o nyom}}, {{о ней|o ney}}; adjectives in {{-ом|-om}}, {{-ой|-oy}}

goal.t: Э́то фильм о любви́.
goal.r: Éto fil'm o lyubví.
goal.tr: It's a movie about love.

dialog.tr: What's this book about?
About a big family in Moscow.

dialog.t: Интере́сно. А о ком ты сейча́с ду́маешь? Ты тако́й гру́стный.
dialog.r: Interésno. A o kom ty seychás dúmayesh'? Ty takóy grústnyy.
dialog.tr: Interesting. And who are you thinking about? You look so sad.

dialog.t: О сестре́. Она́ сейча́с в больни́це.
dialog.r: O sestré. Oná seychás v bol'nítse.
dialog.tr: My sister. She's in the hospital.
Oh no… Tell me about her.

blocks.p: {{о|o}} “about” takes the prepositional, the case of {{в|v}} and {{на|na}} for “where” (lesson 9), with the same endings. {{О чём?|O chom?}} “About what?” and {{О ком?|O kom?}} “About whom?” ask about it. Before a vowel, {{о|o}} becomes {{об|ob}}: {{об э́том|ob étom}} “about this”, {{об А́нне|ob Ánne}}.

**Adjectives in the prepositional** end in {{-ом|-om}} (masculine and neuter) or {{-ой|-oy}} (feminine): {{в большо́м до́ме|v bol'shóm dóme}} “in a big house”, {{о но́вой рабо́те|o nóvoy rabóte}} “about the new job”, {{в ру́сском рестора́не|v rússkom restoráne}}. After {{ж|zh}}, {{ш|sh}}, {{ч|ch}}, {{щ|shch}}, when the ending isn't stressed, they are {{-ем|-em}} and {{-ей|-ey}}: {{о хоро́шем фи́льме|o khoróshem fíl'me}}, {{о хоро́шей пого́де|o khoróshey pogóde}}.

**Verbs.** {{говори́ть о|govorít' o}} “talk about”, {{ду́мать о|dúmat' o}} “think about”, {{расска́зывать|rasskázyvat'}} / {{рассказа́ть о|rasskazát' o}} “tell about”, {{мечта́ть о|mechtát' o}} “dream of”, {{знать о|znat' o}} “know about”. And to say what something is about: {{кни́га о…|kníga o…}}, {{фильм о…|fil'm o…}}, {{пе́сня о…|pésnya o…}}. Watch out for {{любо́вь|lyubóv'}} “love”: {{о любви́|o lyubví}}.

lessons.title: Say who you're with
lessons.summary: Say who you live, go and talk with, and what your coffee comes with: “My sister and I are going to the movies.”
lessons.topic: The instrumental case with {{с|s}}: {{-ом|-om}}, {{-ем|-em}}, {{-ой|-oy}}, {{-ей|-ey}}, {{-ью|-'yu}}; {{со мной|so mnoy}}, {{с ним|s nim}}…; {{мы с дру́гом|my s drúgom}}

goal.t: Я иду́ в кино́ с подру́гой. Хо́чешь с на́ми?
goal.r: Ya idú v kinó s podrúgoy. Khóchesh' s námi?
goal.tr: I'm going to the movies with a friend. Want to come with us?

dialog.tr: Do you live alone?
No, with my sister. And you?

dialog.r: Ya zhivú s drúgom. My s nim vméste rabótayem.

blocks.means: the case for “with” (who you're with, what something comes with), for the tool you do something with, and for what someone works as or becomes. It answers {{с кем?|s kem?}} “with whom?” and {{чем?|chem?}} “with what?”.

blocks.p: {{с|s}} “with” takes the **instrumental**, your fifth case. Masculine and neuter words end in {{-ом|-om}}, feminine words in {{-ой|-oy}}:

table: {{с бра́том|s brátom}}, {{с молоко́м|s molokóm}}, {{с учи́телем|s uchítelem}}

blocks.p: After {{ж|zh}}, {{ш|sh}}, {{ч|ch}}, {{щ|shch}} and {{ц|ts}}, an unstressed {{-ом|-om}} or {{-ой|-oy}} is written {{-ем|-em}} or {{-ей|-ey}}: {{с му́жем|s múzhem}}, {{с Ма́шей|s Máshey}}. Adjectives end in {{-ым|-ym}} (masculine) and {{-ой|-oy}} (feminine): {{с но́вым дру́гом|s nóvym drúgom}}, {{с ру́сской подру́гой|s rússkoy podrúgoy}}.

**My friend and I.** Russian says “we with my friend”: {{мы с дру́гом|my s drúgom}} “my friend and I”, {{мы с ней|my s ney}} “she and I”, with the verb in the {{мы|my}} form. And “with” for food and drink: {{чай с лимо́ном|chay s limónom}}, {{ко́фе с молоко́м|kófe s molokóm}}, {{пирожо́к с мя́сом|pirozhók s myásom}}.

lessons.title: Talk about your job and your hobbies
lessons.summary: Say what you work as, what you wanted to be, and what you do in your free time: “I work as a teacher, and I do yoga.”
lessons.topic: The instrumental without {{с|s}}: {{рабо́тать врачо́м|rabótat' vrachóm}}; {{быть|byt'}} and {{стать|stat'}} + instrumental; {{занима́ться спо́ртом|zanimátsa spórtom}}

goal.t: Я рабо́таю программи́стом, а в свобо́дное вре́мя занима́юсь му́зыкой.
goal.r: Ya rabótayu programmístom, a v svobódnoye vrémya zanimáyus' múzykoy.
goal.tr: I work as a programmer, and in my free time I play music.

dialog.tr: What do you do for a living?
I'm a teacher. And you?

dialog.t: Я врач. Но в де́тстве я хоте́ла стать актри́сой!
dialog.r: Ya vrach. No v détstve ya khotéla stat' aktrísoy!
dialog.tr: I'm a doctor. But as a kid I wanted to be an actress!
And do you do theater now?

dialog.t: Нет, сейча́с я занима́юсь йо́гой и пла́ванием.
dialog.r: Net, seychás ya zanimáyus' yógoy i plávaniyem.
dialog.tr: No, now I do yoga and swimming.
And I'm into history.

blocks.p: The instrumental has a second big job: saying what someone **works as or becomes**. {{Кем вы рабо́таете?|Kem vy rabótayete?}}, word for word “As whom do you work?”, means “What do you do for a living?”. The answer is in the instrumental, with no word for “as”: {{Я рабо́таю врачо́м.|Ya rabótayu vrachóm.}} “I work as a doctor.”

**Be and become.** In the present there's no “is”, so the nominative: {{Я врач.|Ya vrach.}} But after the past, the future and the infinitive of {{быть|byt'}}, and always after {{стать|stat'}} “to become”, the job or role goes into the instrumental: {{Он был учи́телем.|On byl uchítelem.}} “He was a teacher.” {{Я хочу́ стать врачо́м.|Ya khochú stat' vrachóm.}} “I want to become a doctor.”

table: {{Она́ хоте́ла стать актри́сой.|Oná khotéla stat' aktrísoy.}}

blocks.p: **Hobbies.** {{занима́ться|zanimátsa}} and the instrumental means “to do, to go in for” a sport, a hobby or a subject: {{занима́ться спо́ртом|zanimátsa spórtom}}, {{му́зыкой|múzykoy}}, {{йо́гой|yógoy}}, {{ру́сским языко́м|rússkim yazykóm}}. It has {{рабо́тать|rabótat'}}'s forms with {{-ся|-sya}} on the end: {{я занима́юсь|ya zanimáyus'}}, {{ты занима́ешься|ty zanimáyesh'sya}}, {{он занима́ется|on zanimáyetsa}} (lesson 33 explains {{-ся|-sya}}). {{интересова́ться|interesovátsa}} “to be interested in” works the same way: {{я интересу́юсь исто́рией|ya interesúyus' istóriyey}}. And {{Чем ты занима́ешься?|Chem ty zanimáyesh'sya?}} asks “What do you do?”.

ex.tr: What do you want to be? — An engineer.
My father worked as a driver.

ex.t: Я занима́юсь спо́ртом три ра́за в неде́лю.
ex.r: Ya zanimáyus' spórtom tri ráza v nedélyu.
ex.tr: I work out three times a week.

ex.r: Chem ty zanimáyesh'sya v svobódnoye vrémya?
ex.tr: What do you do in your free time?
He's interested in politics.

ex.r: V détstve ya byl óchen' tíkhim rebyónkom.
ex.tr: As a kid I was a very quiet child.

blocks.means: Russian's verbs for going, driving, flying, carrying… They come in pairs: one for going in one direction, one for going there and back, again and again, or around.

blocks.p: In lesson 18, {{идти́|idtí}} and {{е́хать|yékhat'}} meant going somewhere right now, in one direction. Each has a partner for everything else: going regularly, going there and back, moving around in general.

table: again and again; there and back

blocks.p: **Habits.** For something you do regularly, use {{ходи́ть|khodít'}} or {{е́здить|yézdit'}}: {{Я хожу́ в спортза́л три ра́за в неде́лю.|Ya khozhú v sportzál tri ráza v nedélyu.}} {{Ка́ждое ле́то мы е́здим на мо́ре.|Kázhdoye léto my yézdim na móre.}} Compare {{Сейча́с я иду́ в спортза́л.|Seychás ya idú v sportzál.}} “I'm on my way to the gym now.”

**A round trip in the past.** {{Я ходи́л в кино́.|Ya khodíl v kinó.}} means “I went to the movies (and came back)”: it's the usual way to say where you went. {{Мы е́здили в Петербу́рг.|My yézdili v Peterbúrg.}} “We went to St. Petersburg (and we're back).” The past of {{идти́|idtí}}, {{шёл|shol}} / {{шла|shla}}, is “I was walking (somewhere)” at one moment, in the middle of the way.
**On Saturdays.** {{по|po}} with a day in the plural means “on (every) Saturday”: {{по суббо́там|po subbótam}}, {{по понеде́льникам|po ponedél'nikam}}, and {{по утра́м|po utrám}} “in the mornings”.

ex.tr: Do you often go to Moscow?
Yesterday we went to the theater.

ex.t: Где ты была́? — Я ходи́ла в магази́н.
ex.r: Gde ty bylá? — Ya khodíla v magazín.

lessons.title: Get around town: from, to and by
lessons.summary: Say how you get somewhere, where you're coming from and whose place you're going to: “I'm taking the subway to my friend's.”
lessons.topic: {{на авто́бусе|na avtóbuse}}, {{пешко́м|peshkóm}}; {{отку́да?|otkúda?}}: {{из|iz}} and {{с|s}} + genitive; {{к|k}} + dative; {{у|u}} + genitive

goal.t: Я е́ду к дру́гу на метро́.
goal.r: Ya yédu k drúgu na metró.
goal.tr: I'm taking the subway to my friend's place.

dialog.tr: Where are you?

dialog.t: Я е́ду с рабо́ты на авто́бусе.
dialog.r: Ya yédu s rabóty na avtóbuse.
dialog.tr: I'm on the bus, coming from work.
Are you going home?

dialog.t: Нет, снача́ла к Све́те, пото́м домо́й.
dialog.r: Net, snachála k Svéte, potóm domóy.
dialog.tr: No, to Sveta's first, then home.

dialog.t: А когда́ ты бу́дешь у нас?
dialog.r: A kogdá ty búdesh' u nas?
dialog.tr: And when are you coming over to our place?
On Saturday, I promise!

blocks.p: Russian keeps three questions apart: {{где?|gde?}} “where (at)?”, {{куда́?|kudá?}} “where to?” and {{отку́да?|otkúda?}} “where from?”. Each has its own prepositions and cases, and they go in sets:

**Where from?** The opposite of {{в|v}} is {{из|iz}}, and the opposite of {{на|na}} is {{с|s}}; both take the genitive: {{Я из Аме́рики.|Ya iz Amériki.}} “I'm from America.” {{Я иду́ с рабо́ты.|Ya idú s rabóty.}} “I'm coming from work.”

**People's places.** To go to a person, or to their home or office, use {{к|k}} + the dative: {{к дру́гу|k drúgu}} “to my friend's”, {{к врачу́|k vrachú}} “to the doctor”. Being at someone's place is {{у|u}} + the genitive, as in {{у меня́ есть|u menyá yest'}}: {{Я у дру́га.|Ya u drúga.}} “I'm at my friend's.”, {{у нас|u nas}} “at our place”. Coming from a person is {{от|ot}} + the genitive: {{письмо́ от ма́мы|pis'mó ot mámy}} “a letter from Mom”.

**By what?** {{на|na}} and the prepositional: {{на авто́бусе|na avtóbuse}} “by bus”, {{на метро́|na metró}}, {{на такси́|na taksí}}, {{на маши́не|na mashíne}} “by car”, {{на по́езде|na póyezde}} “by train”, {{на самолёте|na samolyóte}} “by plane”. On foot is one word: {{пешко́м|peshkóm}}.

ex.tr: Where are you from? — I'm from Canada.

ex.t: Я е́зжу на рабо́ту на метро́.
ex.r: Ya yézzhu na rabótu na metró.
ex.tr: I take the subway to work.
Tomorrow I'm going to the doctor.

ex.t: В воскресе́нье мы бы́ли у ба́бушки.
ex.r: V voskresén'ye my býli u bábushki.
ex.tr: On Sunday we were at Grandma's.

lessons.title: Count things
lessons.summary: Say how many: five books, twenty minutes, lots of friends, a few questions.
lessons.topic: Numbers with nouns: the genitive plural ({{-ов|-ov}}, {{-ей|-ey}}, no ending); {{ско́лько|skól'ko}}, {{мно́го|mnógo}}, {{ма́ло|málo}}, {{не́сколько|néskol'ko}}

goal.t: У меня́ мно́го друзе́й, но ма́ло вре́мени.
goal.r: U menyá mnógo druzéy, no málo vrémeni.
goal.tr: I have lots of friends but little time.

dialog.tr: How many guests will there be?
About twenty people.

dialog.t: Два́дцать?! А у нас то́лько де́сять сту́льев.
dialog.r: Dvádtsat'?! A u nas tól'ko désyat' stúl'yev.
dialog.tr: Twenty?! But we only have ten chairs.
That's OK, lots of people will stand.
And how many sandwiches?
Fifty. Is that enough?

blocks.p: In lesson 15 you learned {{пять рубле́й|pyat' rubléy}} and {{пять лет|pyat' let}} as set forms. Here's the rule behind them: after 5 and up, and after {{ско́лько|skól'ko}} “how many”, {{мно́го|mnógo}} “many, a lot”, {{ма́ло|málo}} “few, not much” and {{не́сколько|néskol'ko}} “a few, several”, nouns take the **genitive plural**.

**No ending at all.** When dropping the ending would leave two consonants together at the end, a vowel slips in: {{ру́чка|rúchka}} → {{ру́чек|rúchek}}, {{окно́|oknó}} → {{о́кон|ókon}}, {{де́вушка|dévushka}} → {{де́вушек|dévushek}}. Adjectives in the genitive plural end in {{-ых|-ykh}} or {{-их|-ikh}}: {{мно́го краси́вых мест|mnógo krasívykh mest}}.

**The whole rule for numbers.** 1 (21, 31…): the nominative singular. 2, 3, 4 (22, 33…): the genitive singular. 5 to 20, and any number ending in 5 to 9 or 0: the genitive plural. And four everyday words are special: {{челове́к|chelovék}} → {{пять челове́к|pyat' chelovék}} but {{мно́го люде́й|mnógo lyudéy}}; {{год|god}} → {{пять лет|pyat' let}}; {{друг|drug}} → {{друзе́й|druzéy}}; {{ребёнок|rebyónok}} → {{дете́й|detéy}}. And putting the noun before the number makes it rough: {{челове́к два́дцать|chelovék dvádtsat'}} “about twenty people”.

**Much.** Things you can't count stay singular after {{мно́го|mnógo}}, {{ма́ло|málo}} and {{ско́лько|skól'ko}}, in the genitive: {{мно́го вре́мени|mnógo vrémeni}} “a lot of time”, {{ма́ло воды́|málo vodý}} “not much water”.

ex.tr: I've been waiting for twenty minutes!
There are fifteen students in the group.
We have a few questions.
There are lots of beautiful places here.
It costs five thousand rubles.
How many children do you have? — Three.
ex.note: {{тро́е|tróye}}: a word for “three” used for people, especially children

lessons.title: Say whose it is, and ask for amounts
lessons.summary: Say “my brother's car”, “a bottle of water”, “without sugar”, “for you”: the genitive's everyday jobs.
lessons.topic: The genitive for “of”: {{маши́на бра́та|mashína bráta}}, {{буты́лка воды́|butýlka vodý}}; {{без|bez}}, {{для|dlya}}, {{по́сле|pósle}}, {{до|do}}, {{о́коло|ókolo}}

goal.t: Ча́шку ко́фе без са́хара, пожа́луйста.
goal.r: Cháshku kófe bez sákhara, pozháluysta.
goal.tr: A cup of coffee without sugar, please.

dialog.t: Купи́, пожа́луйста, буты́лку молока́ и па́чку ча́я.
dialog.r: Kupí, pozháluysta, butýlku moloká i páchku cháya.
dialog.tr: Please buy a bottle of milk and a pack of tea.
And bread?

dialog.t: Да, и полкило́ сы́ра. Э́то для пирога́.
dialog.r: Da, i polkiló sýra. Éto dlya pirogá.
dialog.tr: Yes, and half a kilo of cheese. It's for the pie.
Where are the car keys?

dialog.t: Вот они́. А э́то ключи́ от маши́ны бра́та.
dialog.r: Vot oní. A éto klyuchí ot mashíny bráta.
dialog.tr: Here they are. And those are the keys to my brother's car.
Got it. I'll be back by nine.

blocks.p: **Of.** Where English says “of” or “'s”, Russian puts the second noun in the genitive, after the first: {{маши́на бра́та|mashína bráta}} “my brother's car” (“the car of the brother”), {{центр го́рода|tsentr góroda}} “the center of town”, {{ключи́ от маши́ны|klyuchí ot mashíny}} “the car keys”.

**Amounts.** Containers and quantities take the genitive too: {{буты́лка воды́|butýlka vodý}} “a bottle of water”, {{ча́шка ча́я|cháshka cháya}} “a cup of tea”, {{кусо́к то́рта|kusók tórta}} “a piece of cake”, {{килогра́мм я́блок|kilográmm yáblok}} “a kilo of apples” (things you count go into the genitive plural). Adjectives join in, with {{-ого|-ogo}} (said -ovo) for masculine and neuter and {{-ой|-oy}} for feminine: {{буты́лка холо́дной воды́|butýlka kholódnoy vodý}}.
**Prepositions with the genitive.** Many common ones take it. You know {{у|u}}, {{из|iz}}, {{с|s}} “from” and {{от|ot}}; here are five more:

ex.tr: This is my brother's car.
I drink my coffee without milk.
This is a present for you.
Let's meet after work.
We live near the park.
Goodbye! — See you tomorrow!

mistakes.why: Russian has no “'s”: the owner goes after, in the genitive.
{{без|bez}} takes the genitive.
“A bottle of”: the genitive.

practice.tr: Can I have a bottle of water?
practice.why: “A bottle of”: {{воды́|vodý}}. ({{буты́лку|butýlku}} is the accusative: the thing you ask for.)

practice.q: In a restaurant: choose your replies.

lines.tr: What will you have to drink?

lines.why: “A bottle of”: the genitive, adjective and all.

practice.tr: After work I'm going to my friend's.

answers.r: Cháshku cháya bez sákhara i kusók tórta dlya podrúgi, pozháluysta.

answers.r: Butýlku vodý i kófe bez moloká, pozháluysta. Éto dlya mámy.
answers.tr: A bottle of water and a coffee without milk, please. It's for my mom.

lessons.title: Describe your daily routine
lessons.summary: Tell someone about your day from morning to night: “I wake up at seven, get dressed and have breakfast.”
lessons.topic: Verbs in {{-ся|-sya}}: {{просыпа́ться|prosypátsa}}, {{одева́ться|odevátsa}}, {{учи́ться|uchítsa}}; {{-ся|-sya}} or {{-сь|-s'}}

goal.t: Я просыпа́юсь в семь, умыва́юсь и одева́юсь.
goal.r: Ya prosypáyus' v sem', umyváyus' i odeváyus'.
goal.tr: I wake up at seven, wash and get dressed.

dialog.tr: What time do you usually get up?

dialog.t: Я просыпа́юсь в шесть, но встаю́ в семь.
dialog.r: Ya prosypáyus' v shest', no vstayú v sem'.
dialog.tr: I wake up at six, but I get up at seven.
And then?

dialog.t: Пото́м принима́ю душ, одева́юсь и за́втракаю.
dialog.r: Potóm prinimáyu dush, odeváyus' i závtrakayu.
dialog.tr: Then I take a shower, get dressed and have breakfast.
And when do you get home?

dialog.t: Часо́в в семь. А в оди́ннадцать ложу́сь спать.
dialog.r: Chasóv v sem'. A v odínnadtsat' lozhús' spat'.
dialog.tr: Around seven. And at eleven I go to bed.

blocks.means: a verb with {{-ся|-sya}} on the end. Often the action is done to yourself (wash yourself, get yourself dressed), but many {{-ся|-sya}} verbs simply come with it.

blocks.p: Many verbs of the daily routine end in {{-ся|-sya}}: {{одева́ться|odevátsa}} “to get dressed” is {{одева́ть|odevát'}} “to dress (someone)” + {{-ся|-sya}} “oneself”. Conjugate the verb as usual and add {{-ся|-sya}} after a consonant, {{-сь|-s'}} after a vowel.

**The day, verb by verb.** {{просыпа́ться|prosypátsa}} “wake up”, {{встава́ть|vstavát'}} “get up” ({{встаю́|vstayú}}, {{встаёшь|vstayósh'}}: no {{-ся|-sya}}), {{умыва́ться|umyvátsa}} “wash (face and hands)”, {{принима́ть душ|prinimát' dush}} “take a shower”, {{одева́ться|odevátsa}} “get dressed”, {{за́втракать|závtrakat'}} “have breakfast”, {{собира́ться|sobirátsa}} “get ready”, {{возвраща́ться|vozvrashchátsa}} “come back”, {{ложи́ться спать|lozhítsa spat'}} “go to bed”. Some {{-ся|-sya}} verbs aren't about yourself at all: {{учи́ться|uchítsa}} “to study”, {{нра́виться|nrávitsa}}, {{занима́ться|zanimátsa}}, {{начина́ться|nachinátsa}} “to begin”, {{конча́ться|konchátsa}} “to end”, {{встреча́ться|vstrechátsa}} “to meet”.
**Linking the steps.** {{снача́ла|snachála}} “first”, {{пото́м|potóm}} “then”, {{по́сле э́того|pósle étovo}} “after that”, {{обы́чно|obýchno}} “usually”, {{иногда́|inogdá}} “sometimes”.

ex.tr: Do you study or work?
I'm a student at the university.
The movie starts at eight.
In the mornings he takes a long time to get ready.
Yesterday I went to bed late.
ex.note: a woman; {{лечь|lech'}} is the perfective of {{ложи́ться|lozhítsa}}

Without {{-ся|-sya}}, you'd be dressing someone else: {{Я одева́ю ребёнка.|Ya odeváyu rebyónka.}}

lessons.title: Talk about dates and birthdays
lessons.summary: Say the date, when your birthday is, when something happened, and how long ago: “My birthday is on May fifth.”
lessons.topic: Ordinal numbers; {{пя́того ма́я|pyátovo máya}}; {{в ма́е|v máye}}; {{в две ты́сячи деся́том году́|v dve týsyachi desyátom godú}}; {{че́рез|chérez}} and {{наза́д|nazád}}

goal.t: У меня́ день рожде́ния пя́того ма́я.
goal.r: U menyá den' rozhdéniya pyátovo máya.
goal.tr: My birthday is on May fifth.

dialog.tr: When's your birthday?
On May fifth. And yours?

dialog.t: Тре́тьего ноября́. А како́е сего́дня число́?
dialog.r: Trét'yevo noyabryá. A kakóye sevódnya chisló?
dialog.tr: On November third. What's the date today?
Today is April twenty-eighth.

dialog.t: Зна́чит, твой день рожде́ния че́рез неде́лю!
dialog.r: Znáchit, tvoy den' rozhdéniya chérez nedélyu!
dialog.tr: So your birthday is in a week!
Yes! Come over!

blocks.means: a number for order: first, second, third.

blocks.p: Russian ordinal numbers are adjectives, with adjective endings: {{пе́рвый|pérvyy}}, {{второ́й|vtoróy}}, {{тре́тий|trétiy}}, {{четвёртый|chetvyórtyy}}, {{пя́тый|pyátyy}}, {{шесто́й|shestóy}}, {{седьмо́й|sed'móy}}, {{восьмо́й|vos'móy}}, {{девя́тый|devyátyy}}, {{деся́тый|desyátyy}}… {{двадца́тый|dvadtsátyy}}, {{тридца́тый|tridtsátyy}}. In a longer number only the last word is an ordinal: {{два́дцать пе́рвый|dvádtsat' pérvyy}} “twenty-first”.

**The date.** {{Како́е сего́дня число́?|Kakóye sevódnya chisló?}} “What's the date today?”. The day is a neuter ordinal (it agrees with {{число́|chisló}} “date”), and the month is in the genitive: {{Сего́дня пе́рвое ма́я.|Sevódnya pérvoye máya.}} “Today is May first.” “On” a date puts the ordinal in the genitive too: {{пе́рвого ма́я|pérvovo máya}} “on May first”. “In” a month is {{в|v}} + the prepositional: {{в ма́е|v máye}}.

**Years.** “In 2010” is {{в|v}}, the ordinal in the prepositional, and {{году́|godú}}: {{в две ты́сячи деся́том году́|v dve týsyachi desyátom godú}}, word for word “in the two-thousand tenth year”. For the 1900s: {{в ты́сяча девятьсо́т девяно́стом году́|v týsyacha devyat'sót devyanóstom godú}} (in 1990). In writing, Russians use digits: {{в 2010 году́|v 2010 godú}}.

**In a week, a week ago.** {{че́рез|chérez}} + the accusative is “in (a time from now)”: {{че́рез неде́лю|chérez nedélyu}} “in a week”, {{че́рез два часа́|chérez dva chasá}} “in two hours”. The time + {{наза́д|nazád}} is “ago”: {{год наза́д|god nazád}} “a year ago”, {{три дня наза́д|tri dnya nazád}} “three days ago”.

ex.t: Я роди́лся в ты́сяча девятьсо́т девяно́сто пе́рвом году́.
ex.r: Ya rodílsya v týsyacha devyat'sót devyanósto pérvom godú.
ex.tr: I was born in 1991.

ex.t: Мы прие́хали в Москву́ в сентябре́.
ex.r: My priyékhali v Moskvú v sentyabré.
ex.tr: We came to Moscow in September.
Today is September first.
ex.note: the first day of school in Russia

ex.tr: The conference is in a month.

ex.t: Я был в Росси́и два го́да наза́д.
ex.r: Ya byl v Rossíi dva góda nazád.
ex.tr: I was in Russia two years ago.

mistakes.tr: My birthday is on May fifth.

“In May”: {{в|v}} + the prepositional.

mistakes.right: Я был там два го́да наза́д.

mistakes.why: {{наза́д|nazád}} comes after the time.

lessons.title: Compare things
lessons.summary: Say what's bigger, cheaper or better, and what's the best: “The subway is faster than the bus.”
lessons.topic: Comparatives ({{-ее|-eye}}, {{лу́чше|lúchshe}}, {{бо́льше|ból'she}}…), {{чем|chem}}, {{гора́здо|gorázdo}}; {{са́мый|sámyy}}

goal.t: Метро́ быстре́е, чем авто́бус.
goal.r: Metró bystréye, chem avtóbus.
goal.tr: The subway is faster than the bus.

dialog.t: Но втора́я деше́вле. И она́ бли́же к метро́.

dialog.tr: But the second one is cheaper. And it's closer to the subway.
Yes, but the first one is much nicer.

dialog.t: Ла́дно, дава́й посмо́трим тре́тью. Говоря́т, она́ са́мая удо́бная!
dialog.r: Ládno, daváy posmótrim trét'yu. Govoryát, oná sámaya udóbnaya!
dialog.tr: OK, let's see the third one. They say it's the most convenient!

blocks.p: **-er.** To compare, most adjectives drop their ending and add {{-ее|-eye}}: {{бы́стрый|býstryy}} → {{быстре́е|bystréye}} “faster”, {{интере́сный|interésnyy}} → {{интере́снее|interésneye}}, {{тёплый|tyóplyy}} → {{тепле́е|tepléye}}. This form doesn't change for gender or number ({{Э́тот дом краси́вее. Э́та кварти́ра краси́вее.|Étot dom krasíveye. Éta kvartíra krasíveye.}}), and it's also the adverb: {{Говори́те ме́дленнее.|Govoríte médlenneye.}} “Speak more slowly.”

**Than.** Two ways. {{чем|chem}}, with a comma before it: {{Метро́ быстре́е, чем авто́бус.|Metró bystréye, chem avtóbus.}} Or, shorter, the second thing in the genitive with no {{чем|chem}}: {{Метро́ быстре́е авто́буса.|Metró bystréye avtóbusa.}} {{Он ста́рше меня́.|On stárshe menyá.}} “He's older than me.”
**Irregular ones.** Many everyday adjectives have their own short comparative, often with a change of consonant:

**Much, a bit.** {{гора́здо|gorázdo}} or {{намно́го|namnóvo}} “much”: {{гора́здо лу́чше|gorázdo lúchshe}} “much better”; {{немно́го|nemnógo}} “a bit”: {{немно́го деше́вле|nemnógo deshévle}}. And {{бо́льше|ból'she}} and {{ме́ньше|mén'she}} also mean “more” and “less”: {{Я люблю́ чай бо́льше, чем ко́фе.|Ya lyublyú chay ból'she, chem kófe.}}

**The most.** {{са́мый|sámyy}} and the adjective, both agreeing with the noun: {{са́мый большо́й го́род|sámyy bol'shóy górod}} “the biggest city”, {{са́мая краси́вая у́лица|sámaya krasívaya úlitsa}} “the most beautiful street”. “Best” and “worst” also have their own words: {{лу́чший|lúchshiy}}, {{ху́дший|khúdshiy}}.

ex.t: Москва́ — са́мый большо́й го́род в Росси́и.
ex.r: Moskvá — sámyy bol'shóy górod v Rossíi.
ex.tr: Moscow is the biggest city in Russia.
It's warmer today than yesterday.

ex.t: Мой брат ста́рше меня́ на три го́да.
ex.r: Moy brat stárshe menyá na tri góda.
ex.tr: My brother is three years older than me.
This phone is much more expensive.
This is the best restaurant in town.

mistakes.why: {{большо́й|bol'shóy}} has its own comparative: {{бо́льше|ból'she}}.
Either {{чем я|chem ya}}, or the genitive {{меня́|menyá}} with no {{чем|chem}}.
“The best” is {{лу́чший|lúchshiy}}, an adjective that agrees. {{лу́чше|lúchshe}} is “better”.

practice.tr: This is the tallest building in town.

practice.q: In a clothes store: choose your replies.

lines.t: Вот э́та. Она́ ме́ньше, но доро́же.
lines.r: Vot éta. Oná mén'she, no dorózhe.
lines.tr: This one. It's smaller, but more expensive.

practice.tr: This is the most beautiful street in Moscow.

practice.q: Say: “My sister is taller than me.”
Your turn: compare two cities, two seasons or two foods. Use a comparative with {{чем|chem}} or the genitive, and {{гора́здо|gorázdo}} if you like.

answers.t: Ле́то лу́чше зимы́: оно́ гора́здо тепле́е.
answers.r: Léto lúchshe zimý: onó gorázdo tepléye.
answers.tr: Summer is better than winter: it's much warmer.

answers.t: Москва́ бо́льше, чем Петербу́рг, но Петербу́рг краси́вее.
answers.r: Moskvá ból'she, chem Peterbúrg, no Peterbúrg krasíveye.
answers.tr: Moscow is bigger than St. Petersburg, but St. Petersburg is more beautiful.

lessons.title: Describe people
lessons.summary: Say what people look like, what they're like, and how they are today: “She has long hair.” “He's busy.” “I'm glad.”
lessons.topic: {{у неё дли́нные во́лосы|u neyó dlínnyye vólosy}}; {{Како́й он?|Kakóy on?}}; short adjectives: {{рад|rad}}, {{за́нят|zányat}}, {{гото́в|gotóv}}, {{бо́лен|bólen}}, {{похо́ж на|pokhózh na}}

goal.t: Она́ высо́кая, у неё дли́нные во́лосы и голубы́е глаза́.
goal.r: Oná vysókaya, u neyó dlínnyye vólosy i golubýye glazá.
goal.tr: She's tall, with long hair and blue eyes.

dialog.t: Ты встре́тишь моего́ бра́та в аэропорту́?
dialog.r: Ty vstrétish' moyevó bráta v aeroportú?
dialog.tr: Will you meet my brother at the airport?
Sure. What does he look like?

dialog.t: Он высо́кий, худо́й, у него́ коро́ткие тёмные во́лосы и борода́.
dialog.r: On vysókiy, khudóy, u nevó korótkiye tyómnyye vólosy i borodá.
dialog.tr: He's tall and thin, with short dark hair and a beard.
And what's he like? Is he chatty?

dialog.t: Нет, он немно́го стесни́тельный, но о́чень до́брый. Он похо́ж на меня́!
dialog.r: Net, on nemnógo stesnítel'nyy, no óchen' dóbryy. On pokhózh na menyá!
dialog.tr: No, he's a bit shy, but very kind. He looks like me!
Then I'll definitely recognize him.

blocks.p: **What someone looks like.** {{Как он вы́глядит?|Kak on výglyadit?}} “What does he look like?”. Features go with {{у|u}} and the person, like {{у меня́ есть|u menyá yest'}}: {{У неё дли́нные во́лосы.|U neyó dlínnyye vólosy.}} “She has long hair.” ({{во́лосы|vólosy}} is plural in Russian.) The person's build is an adjective: {{Он высо́кий.|On vysókiy.}} “He's tall.”

**What someone is like.** {{Како́й он?|Kakóy on?}} “What's he like?” asks about character: {{до́брый|dóbryy}} “kind”, {{весёлый|vesyólyy}} “fun, cheerful”, {{у́мный|úmnyy}} “smart”, {{серьёзный|ser'yóznyy}} “serious”, {{стесни́тельный|stesnítel'nyy}} “shy”, {{разгово́рчивый|razgovórchivyy}} “chatty”.

blocks.means: a short form of some adjectives, used after the noun to say how someone or something is (often just now): {{Он за́нят.|On zányat.}} “He's busy.”

blocks.p: **How someone is right now.** A few common words are nearly always short, after the noun, with endings like the past tense: nothing for a man, {{-а|-a}} for a woman, {{-ы|-y}} for several people and for polite {{вы|vy}}.
**Looks like.** {{похо́ж на|pokhózh na}} + the accusative: {{Он похо́ж на ма́му.|On pokhózh na mámu.}} “He looks like his mom.” ({{похо́жа|pokhózha}} for a woman, {{похо́жи|pokhózhi}} for several.)

ex.tr: I'm so glad to see you!
Sorry, I'm busy right now.

ex.t: У него́ ка́рие глаза́ и све́тлые во́лосы.
ex.r: U nevó káriye glazá i svétlyye vólosy.
ex.tr: He has brown eyes and fair hair.
Are you ready? — Yes, let's go!
You're right.
The children look a lot like their father.

mistakes.why: Features: {{у|u}} and the person, as with {{у меня́ есть|u menyá yest'}}.

mistakes.tr: I'm glad to see you! (a woman speaking)
mistakes.why: A woman says {{ра́да|ráda}}: short adjectives follow the gender.
{{похо́ж на|pokhózh na}} + the accusative.

practice.q: You're a man. A friend asks about the new neighbor. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: Do you know the new neighbor?

options: Да, я её ви́дел. Она́ невысо́кая, у неё коро́ткие во́лосы.
Да, я её ви́дел. Она́ име́ет коро́ткие во́лосы.
rs: Da, ya yeyó vídel. Oná nevysókaya, u neyó korótkiye vólosy.
Da, ya yeyó vídel. Oná iméyet korótkiye vólosy.

options: О́чень весёлая. Мы с ней до́лго говори́ли.
О́чень весёлая. Мы с она́ до́лго говори́ли.
rs: Óchen' vesyólaya. My s ney dólgo govoríli.
Óchen' vesyólaya. My s oná dólgo govoríli.
lines.why: “She and I”: {{мы с ней|my s ney}}.

practice.tr: My sister is taller than me.

practice.q: Say, as a man: “I'm so glad to see you!”
Your turn: describe someone you know: what they look like and what they're like. Use {{у него́ / у неё…|u nevó / u neyó…}}, adjectives, and {{похо́ж(а) на|pokhózh(a) na}} if you like.

answers.t: Мой брат высо́кий, у него́ тёмные во́лосы. Он о́чень до́брый и похо́ж на па́пу.
answers.r: Moy brat vysókiy, u nevó tyómnyye vólosy. On óchen' dóbryy i pokhózh na pápu.
answers.tr: My brother is tall, with dark hair. He's very kind and looks like Dad.

answers.t: Моя́ подру́га невысо́кая, у неё голубы́е глаза́. Она́ весёлая и разгово́рчивая.
answers.r: Moyá podrúga nevysókaya, u neyó golubýye glazá. Oná vesyólaya i razgovórchivaya.
answers.tr: My friend is short, with blue eyes. She's fun and chatty.

lessons.title: Give advice and say what must be done
lessons.summary: Tell someone what they should, must and mustn't do: “You should get some rest.” “You can't park here.”
lessons.topic: {{до́лжен|dólzhen}}, {{должна́|dolzhná}}, {{должны́|dolzhný}}; {{сто́ит|stóit}} and {{лу́чше|lúchshe}} + infinitive; {{не на́до|ne nádo}} and {{нельзя́|nel'zyá}} with the right aspect

goal.t: Тебе́ сто́ит отдохну́ть. Ты до́лжен бо́льше спать.
goal.r: Tebé stóit otdokhnút'. Ty dólzhen ból'she spat'.
goal.tr: You should get some rest. You need to sleep more.
goal.note: to a man; to a woman, {{ты должна́|ty dolzhná}}

dialog.tr: What's the matter?

dialog.t: У меня́ боли́т голова́, и я пло́хо сплю.
dialog.r: U menyá bolít golová, i ya plókho splyu.
dialog.tr: I have a headache, and I'm sleeping badly.
Do you work a lot?

dialog.t: Да, по двена́дцать часо́в в день.
dialog.r: Da, po dvenádtsat' chasóv v den'.
dialog.tr: Yes, twelve hours a day.

dialog.t: Вам на́до отдыха́ть. Вы должны́ спать во́семь часо́в и бо́льше гуля́ть.
dialog.r: Vam nádo otdykhát'. Vy dolzhný spat' vósem' chasóv i ból'she gulyát'.
dialog.tr: You need to rest. You must sleep eight hours and walk more.
And can I have coffee?

dialog.t: Мо́жно, но ве́чером лу́чше не пить.
dialog.r: Mózhno, no vécherom lúchshe ne pit'.
dialog.tr: You can, but better not drink it in the evening.

blocks.p: **Must.** {{до́лжен|dólzhen}} “must, have to, be supposed to” is a short adjective, like {{рад|rad}} and {{за́нят|zányat}}, so it agrees with the person: {{я до́лжен|ya dólzhen}} (a man), {{я должна́|ya dolzhná}} (a woman), {{мы должны́|my dolzhný}}. Then comes the infinitive: {{Ты должна́ позвони́ть ма́ме.|Ty dolzhná pozvonít' máme.}} “You must call Mom.” It's firmer than {{на́до|nádo}}: a duty, an obligation.

**Advice.** {{Тебе́ сто́ит…|Tebé stóit…}} “You should…, it's worth…” and {{Лу́чше…|Lúchshe…}} “Better…” take an infinitive, with the person in the dative: {{Вам сто́ит посмотре́ть э́тот фильм.|Vam stóit posmotrét' étot fil'm.}} {{Лу́чше е́хать на метро́.|Lúchshe yékhat' na metró.}} “Better take the subway.”

**Don't and mustn't: watch the aspect.** {{не на́до|ne nádo}} + the imperfective is “no need to, don't”: {{Не на́до покупа́ть хлеб.|Ne nádo pokupát' khleb.}} “Don't buy bread (we have some).” {{нельзя́|nel'zyá}} + the imperfective is “it's not allowed”: {{Здесь нельзя́ кури́ть.|Zdes' nel'zyá kurít'.}} But {{нельзя́|nel'zyá}} + the perfective is “it's impossible”: {{Окно́ нельзя́ откры́ть.|Oknó nel'zyá otkrýt'.}} “The window won't open.”

ex.tr: I have to go, sorry.
You should try borscht.
Better call him tomorrow.
There's no need to worry.
You can't park here.
We have to finish by Friday.

mistakes.why: {{до́лжен|dólzhen}} agrees: {{должна́|dolzhná}} for a woman.
{{до́лжен|dólzhen}} goes with the subject {{ты|ty}}; the dative {{тебе́|tebé}} goes with {{на́до|nádo}} and {{сто́ит|stóit}}.
After {{не на́до|ne nádo}}: the imperfective.

practice.t: Не на́до ___ такси́, я тебя́ отвезу́.
practice.r: Ne nádo ___ taksí, ya tebyá otvezú.
practice.tr: No need to call a taxi, I'll drive you.

options: You're not allowed to open the window.
practice.why: {{нельзя́|nel'zyá}} + the perfective: impossible. “Not allowed” is {{нельзя́ открыва́ть|nel'zyá otkryvát'}}.

practice.q: A friend feels sick. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: I feel awful. I think I'm sick.

options: Тебе́ на́до к врачу́! И лу́чше лечь.
Тебе́ на́до к врач! И лу́чше лёг.
rs: Tebé nádo k vrachú! I lúchshe lech'.
Tebé nádo k vrach! I lúchshe lyog.
lines.why: To a person: {{к врачу́|k vrachú}}. After {{лу́чше|lúchshe}}: the infinitive {{лечь|lech'}}.

lines.tr: And can I go to work?

options: Нет, не на́до идти́ на рабо́ту.
Нет, не на́до пойти́ на рабо́ту.
rs: Net, ne nádo idtí na rabótu.
Net, ne nádo poytí na rabótu.

practice.q: Your turn: a friend is tired and stressed. Give them three pieces of advice with {{тебе́ сто́ит|tebé stóit}}, {{ты до́лжен / должна́|ty dólzhen / dolzhná}} and {{не на́до|ne nádo}}.

answers.t: Тебе́ сто́ит отдохну́ть. Ты до́лжен бо́льше спать. Не на́до так мно́го рабо́тать!
answers.r: Tebé stóit otdokhnút'. Ty dólzhen ból'she spat'. Ne nádo tak mnógo rabótat'!
answers.tr: You should get some rest. You need to sleep more. Don't work so much!

answers.t: Тебе́ сто́ит пое́хать на мо́ре. Ты должна́ ду́мать о себе́. И не на́до пить сто́лько ко́фе!
answers.r: Tebé stóit poyékhat' na móre. Ty dolzhná dúmat' o sebé. I ne nádo pit' stól'ko kófe!
answers.tr: You should go to the seaside. You need to think about yourself. And don't drink so much coffee!

lessons.title: Say why
lessons.summary: Give reasons and results: “I stayed home because it was raining, so I watched a movie.”
lessons.topic: {{Почему́?|Pochemú?}} {{Потому́ что…|Potomú shto…}}; {{поэ́тому|poétomu}}; {{так как|tak kak}}; {{из-за|iz-za}} + genitive, {{благодаря́|blagodaryá}} + dative

goal.t: Я не пришёл, потому́ что был бо́лен.
goal.r: Ya ne prishól, potomú shto byl bólen.
goal.tr: I didn't come because I was sick.
goal.note: a man; a woman says {{не пришла́|ne prishlá}}, {{была́ больна́|bylá bol'ná}}

dialog.tr: Why are you late?
Sorry, my bus broke down.
Again?

dialog.t: Да, из-за сне́га все авто́бусы опа́здывают. Поэ́тому за́втра я пое́ду на метро́.
dialog.r: Da, iz-za snéga vse avtóbusy opázdyvayut. Poétomu závtra ya poyédu na metró.
dialog.tr: Yes, all the buses are late because of the snow. So tomorrow I'll take the subway.
Good idea.

blocks.p: **Because.** {{Почему́?|Pochemú?}} “Why?” — {{Потому́ что…|Potomú shto…}} “Because…”. In writing there's a comma before it: {{Я до́ма, потому́ что идёт дождь.|Ya dóma, potomú shto idyót dozhd'.}} “I'm home because it's raining.” {{так как|tak kak}} “since, as” means the same, sounds a little more formal, and can start the sentence: {{Так как бы́ло по́здно, мы взя́ли такси́.|Tak kak býlo pózno, my vzyáli taksí.}}

**So.** {{поэ́тому|poétomu}} “so, that's why” introduces the result: {{Идёт дождь, поэ́тому я до́ма.|Idyót dozhd', poétomu ya dóma.}} The two are easy to mix up: the reason comes after {{потому́ что|potomú shto}}, the result after {{поэ́тому|poétomu}}.

table: {{Шёл дождь, поэ́тому мы оста́лись до́ма.|Shol dozhd', poétomu my ostális' dóma.}}
{{Мы оста́лись до́ма, потому́ что шёл дождь.|My ostális' dóma, potomú shto shol dozhd'.}}

blocks.p: **Because of + a noun.** {{из-за|iz-za}} + the genitive for a cause that is bad or neutral: {{из-за сне́га|iz-za snéga}} “because of the snow”, {{из-за тебя́|iz-za tebyá}} “because of you” (it's your fault!). {{благодаря́|blagodaryá}} + the dative for a good one: {{благодаря́ тебе́|blagodaryá tebé}} “thanks to you”.

**What for?** {{Заче́м?|Zachém?}} asks about the purpose, {{почему́?|pochemú?}} about the cause: {{Заче́м ты у́чишь ру́сский?|Zachém ty úchish' rússkiy?}} “What are you learning Russian for?”. A later lesson shows how to answer it with {{что́бы|shtóby}} “in order to”.

ex.t: Почему́ ты не спишь? — Потому́ что за́втра экза́мен.
ex.r: Pochemú ty ne spish'? — Potomú shto závtra ekzámen.
ex.tr: Why aren't you asleep? — Because there's an exam tomorrow.

ex.t: Я уста́л, поэ́тому ра́но лёг спать.
ex.r: Ya ustál, poétomu ráno lyog spat'.
ex.tr: I was tired, so I went to bed early.

ex.t: Из-за рабо́ты я не могу́ прийти́.
ex.r: Iz-za rabóty ya ne mogú priytí.
ex.tr: I can't come because of work.
Thanks to you I passed the exam.

ex.t: Так как у нас ма́ло вре́мени, начнём.
ex.r: Tak kak u nas málo vrémeni, nachnyóm.
ex.tr: Since we don't have much time, let's begin.

mistakes.right: Я до́ма, потому́ что идёт дождь.
mistakes.why: The rain is the reason: {{потому́ что|potomú shto}}. {{поэ́тому|poétomu}} introduces the result.

mistakes.tr: Thanks to you I passed the exam!
mistakes.why: A good cause: {{благодаря́|blagodaryá}} + the dative. {{из-за|iz-za}} sounds like blame.

practice.tr: I didn't call because my phone died.

practice.t: Бы́ло хо́лодно, ___ мы не пошли́ гуля́ть.
practice.r: Býlo khólodno, ___ my ne poshlí gulyát'.
practice.tr: It was cold, so we didn't go for a walk.
We were late because of the traffic.

practice.q: A friend helped you get a job. You say…
You're a woman. A friend asks why you didn't come. Choose your replies.

lines.why: The reason: {{потому́ что|potomú shto}}; and a woman is {{больна́|bol'ná}}.

lines.tr: Oh no! How are you now?

practice.q: Your turn: why are you learning Russian? Give a reason with {{потому́ что|potomú shto}} and a result with {{поэ́тому|poétomu}}.

answers.t: Я учу́ ру́сский, потому́ что моя́ жена́ ру́сская. Поэ́тому я хочу́ говори́ть с её ма́мой.
answers.r: Ya uchú rússkiy, potomú shto moyá zhená rússkaya. Poétomu ya khochú govorít' s yeyó mámoy.
answers.tr: I'm learning Russian because my wife is Russian. That's why I want to talk to her mom.

answers.t: Мне нра́вится ру́сская литерату́ра, поэ́тому я хочу́ чита́ть Толсто́го по-ру́сски.
answers.r: Mne nrávitsa rússkaya literatúra, poétomu ya khochú chitát' Tolstóvo po-rússki.
answers.tr: I love Russian literature, so I want to read Tolstoy in Russian.

lessons.title: Say what will happen if…
lessons.summary: Make plans that depend on something: “If it rains, we'll stay home.” “When I get there, I'll call you.”
lessons.topic: {{е́сли|yésli}} and {{когда́|kogdá}} + the future, where English uses the present

goal.t: Е́сли за́втра бу́дет хоро́шая пого́да, мы пое́дем на пляж.
goal.r: Yésli závtra búdet khoróshaya pogóda, my poyédem na plyazh.
goal.tr: If the weather's nice tomorrow, we'll go to the beach.

dialog.t: Что вы бу́дете де́лать в суббо́ту?
dialog.r: Shto vy búdete délat' v subbótu?
dialog.tr: What are you doing on Saturday?

dialog.t: Е́сли бу́дет со́лнце, пое́дем на да́чу. А е́сли бу́дет дождь, пойдём в музе́й.
dialog.r: Yésli búdet sóntse, poyédem na dáchu. A yésli búdet dozhd', poydyóm v muzéy.
dialog.tr: If it's sunny, we'll go to the dacha. And if it rains, we'll go to a museum.
And when will you be back?
When we get back, I'll call you.
Deal!

blocks.p: **English and Russian disagree here.** English says “If it rains, we'll stay home”, with the present after “if”. Russian is logical: the rain is in the future, so the verb is too: {{Е́сли бу́дет дождь, мы оста́немся до́ма.|Yésli búdet dozhd', my ostánemsya dóma.}} The same after {{когда́|kogdá}} “when” about the future: {{Когда́ я прие́ду, я позвоню́.|Kogdá ya priyédu, ya pozvonyú.}} “When I arrive, I'll call.”

table: {{Е́сли бу́дет дождь, мы оста́немся до́ма.|Yésli búdet dozhd', my ostánemsya dóma.}}
When I **get** home, I'll call you.
{{Когда́ я приду́ домо́й, я тебе́ позвоню́.|Kogdá ya pridú domóy, ya tebé pozvonyú.}}
{{Е́сли у тебя́ бу́дет вре́мя, позвони́ мне.|Yésli u tebyá búdet vrémya, pozvoní mne.}}

blocks.p: **Which future?** The aspect rules you know: one event with a result is perfective ({{Е́сли ты придёшь…|Yésli ty pridyósh'…}} “If you come…”); something going on is {{бу́ду|búdu}} + the imperfective ({{Е́сли ты бу́дешь рабо́тать ве́чером…|Yésli ty búdesh' rabótat' vécherom…}} “If you're working tonight…”); and a state is {{бу́дет|búdet}} ({{е́сли бу́дет вре́мя|yésli búdet vrémya}} “if there's time”).

**Always true, or true now.** For things that are always true, or true right now, both languages use the present: {{Е́сли я пью ко́фе ве́чером, я пло́хо сплю.|Yésli ya p'yu kófe vécherom, ya plókho splyu.}} “If I drink coffee in the evening, I sleep badly.” {{Е́сли ты хо́чешь, я помогу́.|Yésli ty khóchesh', ya pomogú.}} “If you want, I'll help.”

ex.t: Когда́ я зако́нчу рабо́ту, я тебе́ напишу́.
ex.r: Kogdá ya zakónchu rabótu, ya tebé napishú.
ex.tr: When I finish work, I'll text you.
If it's cold, put on a hat.

ex.t: Е́сли ты опозда́ешь, мы уйдём без тебя́.
ex.r: Yésli ty opozdáyesh', my uydyóm bez tebyá.
ex.tr: If you're late, we'll leave without you.
Call when you're home.

ex.t: Е́сли ты хо́чешь, я тебе́ помогу́.
ex.r: Yésli ty khóchesh', ya tebé pomogú.
ex.tr: If you want, I'll help you.
ex.note: you want it now: the present

mistakes.wrong: Е́сли за́втра идёт дождь, мы оста́немся до́ма.
mistakes.right: Е́сли за́втра бу́дет дождь, мы оста́немся до́ма.
mistakes.tr: If it rains tomorrow, we'll stay home.
mistakes.why: Tomorrow's rain is in the future: {{бу́дет дождь|búdet dozhd'}}.

mistakes.wrong: Когда́ я прихожу́ домо́й, я позвоню́.
mistakes.right: Когда́ я приду́ домо́й, я позвоню́.
mistakes.tr: When I get home, I'll call.
mistakes.why: A future arrival: the perfective future {{приду́|pridú}}.

practice.t: Е́сли за́втра ___ хоро́шая пого́да, мы пойдём гуля́ть.
practice.r: Yésli závtra ___ khoróshaya pogóda, my poydyóm gulyát'.
practice.tr: If the weather's nice tomorrow, we'll go for a walk.

practice.tr: When I get to Moscow, I'll call you.

{{Когда́ я прихожу́ домо́й, я позвоню́.|Kogdá ya prikhozhú domóy, ya pozvonyú.}}
practice.why: After {{когда́|kogdá}}, a future event takes the future.

practice.answer: Е́сли бу́дет дождь, мы оста́немся до́ма.

answers.r: Yésli búdet tepló, my poydyóm na plyazh. Yésli búdet khólodno, ostánemsya dóma.
answers.tr: If it's warm, we'll go to the beach. If it's cold, we'll stay home.

lessons.title: Talk about experiences: ever and never
lessons.summary: Ask “Have you ever…?” and answer with “never”, “nobody” and “nothing”: Russian's double negatives.
lessons.topic: {{никогда́ не|nikogdá ne}}, {{никто́ не|niktó ne}}, {{ничего́ не|nichevó ne}}: two negatives in one sentence; {{когда́-нибудь|kogdá-nibud'}}

goal.t: Я никогда́ не был в Росси́и.
goal.r: Ya nikogdá ne byl v Rossíi.
goal.tr: I've never been to Russia.
goal.note: a man; a woman says {{не была́|ne bylá}}

dialog.tr: Have you ever been to Russia?

dialog.t: Нет, никогда́ не был. А ты был в Аме́рике?
dialog.r: Net, nikogdá ne byl. A ty byl v Amérike?
dialog.tr: No, never. And have you been to America?

dialog.t: Был, оди́н раз. Но я там никого́ не знал и ничего́ не понима́л!
dialog.r: Byl, odín raz. No ya tam nikovó ne znal i nichevó ne ponimál!
dialog.tr: Once. But I didn't know anybody there and didn't understand anything!

dialog.t: А сейча́с ты хорошо́ говори́шь по-англи́йски.
dialog.r: A seychás ty khoroshó govorísh' po-anglíyski.
dialog.tr: But now you speak English well.

dialog.t: Спаси́бо! Но я никогда́ не говорю́ без оши́бок.
dialog.r: Spasíbo! No ya nikogdá ne govoryú bez oshíbok.
dialog.tr: Thanks! But I never speak without mistakes.

blocks.p: **Two negatives make a negative.** English says “I never saw anyone”, with one negative word. Russian puts {{не|ne}} before the verb **as well as** a “no-” word, and the sentence is still negative, only stronger: {{Я никогда́ не был в Росси́и.|Ya nikogdá ne byl v Rossíi.}} “I've never been to Russia.” {{Никто́ не зна́ет.|Niktó ne znáyet.}} “Nobody knows.” {{Я ничего́ не ви́жу.|Ya nichevó ne vízhu.}} “I can't see anything.” You can even stack them: {{Никто́ никогда́ ничего́ не говори́т.|Niktó nikogdá nichevó ne govorít.}} “Nobody ever says anything.”

table: {{Я никогда́ не опа́здываю.|Ya nikogdá ne opázdyvayu.}}
{{Я ничего́ не зна́ю.|Ya nichevó ne znáyu.}}
{{Я нигде́ не мог найти́ ключи́.|Ya nigdé ne mog naytí klyuchí.}}
{{Сего́дня я никуда́ не иду́.|Sevódnya ya nikudá ne idú.}}

blocks.p: **They change like {{кто|kto}} and {{что|shto}}.** {{никто́|niktó}} has the cases of {{кто|kto}}: {{никого́|nikovó}} (accusative and genitive), {{никому́|nikomú}} (dative). “Nothing” is usually {{ничего́|nichevó}}. With a preposition, it goes in the middle: {{ни с кем|ni s kem}} “with nobody”, {{ни о чём|ni o chom}} “about nothing”.

**Ever.** In a question, “ever” is {{когда́-нибудь|kogdá-nibud'}}: {{Ты когда́-нибудь был в Росси́и?|Ty kogdá-nibud' byl v Rossíi?}} The same {{-нибудь|-nibud'}} makes “any-” words: {{кто́-нибудь|któ-nibud'}} “anybody”, {{что́-нибудь|shtó-nibud'}} “anything”, {{где́-нибудь|gdé-nibud'}} “anywhere”. In a “no” answer they become “no-” words: {{Ты что́-нибудь зна́ешь? — Нет, я ничего́ не зна́ю.|Ty shtó-nibud' znáyesh'? — Net, ya nichevó ne znáyu.}}

ex.t: Ты когда́-нибудь ел борщ? — Нет, никогда́.
ex.r: Ty kogdá-nibud' yel borshch? — Net, nikogdá.
ex.tr: Have you ever had borscht? — No, never.
Nobody knows where he is.
I won't tell anyone.
I don't need anything, thanks.

ex.t: Она́ ни с кем не говори́т.
ex.r: Oná ni s kem ne govorít.
ex.tr: She isn't talking to anyone.
Does anyone want coffee?

mistakes.right: Я никогда́ не был в Москве́.
mistakes.why: With {{никогда́|nikogdá}}, {{никто́|niktó}}, {{ничего́|nichevó}}, the verb still needs {{не|ne}}.
In a negative sentence, “anything” is {{ничего́|nichevó}}.
{{никто́|niktó}} takes a singular verb, like {{кто|kto}}.

practice.tr: Have you seen my glasses anywhere?

practice.q: {{Я ничего́ не понима́ю|Ya nichevó ne ponimáyu}} means…
You're a man. Monday morning: choose your replies.

lines.tr: What did you do on the weekend?

practice.q: Your turn: say something you've never done, and ask a friend if they've ever done something. Use {{никогда́ не|nikogdá ne}} and {{когда́-нибудь|kogdá-nibud'}}.

answers.t: Я никогда́ не был в Москве́ и никогда́ не ел икру́. А ты когда́-нибудь пры́гал с парашю́том?
answers.r: Ya nikogdá ne byl v Moskvé i nikogdá ne yel ikrú. A ty kogdá-nibud' prýgal s parashyútom?
answers.tr: I've never been to Moscow and never eaten caviar. Have you ever gone skydiving?

answers.t: Я никогда́ не ви́дела сне́га. А ты когда́-нибудь ката́лся на лы́жах?
answers.r: Ya nikogdá ne vídela snéga. A ty kogdá-nibud' katálsya na lýzhakh?
answers.tr: I've never seen snow. Have you ever been skiing?

lessons.title: Tell what happened, in order
lessons.summary: Tell a short story: what was going on, what happened next and how it ended. Aspect in a story.
lessons.topic: Aspect in a story: perfective for the events, imperfective for the background; {{снача́ла|snachála}}, {{пото́м|potóm}}, {{вдруг|vdrug}}, {{когда́|kogdá}}

goal.t: Я шёл домо́й, когда́ вдруг уви́дел ста́рого дру́га.
goal.r: Ya shol domóy, kogdá vdrug uvídel stárovo drúga.
goal.tr: I was walking home when suddenly I saw an old friend.

dialog.tr: Come on, tell me! What happened?

dialog.t: Вчера́ я е́хал в метро́ и чита́л кни́гу.
dialog.r: Vcherá ya yékhal v metró i chitál knígu.
dialog.tr: Yesterday I was riding the subway, reading a book.

dialog.t: Вдруг ко мне подошла́ де́вушка и спроси́ла, что я чита́ю.
dialog.r: Vdrug ko mne podoshlá dévushka i sprosíla, shto ya chitáyu.
dialog.tr: Suddenly a girl came up to me and asked what I was reading.
And what did you say?

dialog.t: Я показа́л ей кни́гу. Мы разговори́лись, и тепе́рь у меня́ есть её но́мер!
dialog.r: Ya pokazál yey knígu. My razgovorílis', i tepér' u menyá yest' yeyó nómer!
dialog.tr: I showed her the book. We got talking, and now I have her number!
Wow!

blocks.p: A story uses both aspects, each for its own job. The **perfective** moves the story forward: one finished event after another, {{пришёл|prishól}}, {{сел|sel}}, {{откры́л|otkrýl}}. The **imperfective** paints the background, what was going on when the events happened: {{шёл дождь|shol dozhd'}} “it was raining”, {{я чита́л|ya chitál}} “I was reading”.

table: {{Я е́хал в метро́…|Ya yékhal v metró…}}
{{Вдруг ко мне подошла́ де́вушка.|Vdrug ko mne podoshlá dévushka.}}

blocks.p: **Two events in a row** are two perfectives: {{Он пришёл, сел и откры́л ноутбу́к.|On prishól, sel i otkrýl noutbúk.}} “He came in, sat down and opened his laptop.” **Two things at the same time** are two imperfectives: {{Я гото́вил у́жин и слу́шал му́зыку.|Ya gotóvil úzhin i slúshal múzyku.}} “I was cooking dinner and listening to music.” And **an event during a background** is one of each: {{Когда́ я гуля́л в па́рке, я уви́дел ста́рого дру́га.|Kogdá ya gulyál v párke, ya uvídel stárovo drúga.}}

**Linking words.** {{снача́ла|snachála}} “first”, {{пото́м|potóm}} and {{зате́м|zatém}} “then”, {{по́сле э́того|pósle étovo}} “after that”, {{вдруг|vdrug}} “suddenly”, {{в конце́ концо́в|v kontsé kontsóv}} “in the end”, {{наконе́ц|nakonéts}} “at last”. And for the listener: {{Что случи́лось?|Shto sluchílos'?}} “What happened?”.

ex.t: Снача́ла мы погуля́ли, пото́м пошли́ в кафе́.
ex.r: Snachála my pogulyáli, potóm poshlí v kafé.
ex.tr: First we went for a walk, then we went to a café.

ex.t: Когда́ я пришёл домо́й, де́ти уже́ спа́ли.
ex.r: Kogdá ya prishól domóy, déti uzhé spáli.
ex.tr: When I got home, the kids were already asleep.

ex.t: Мы сиде́ли в кафе́, когда́ начался́ дождь.
ex.r: My sidéli v kafé, kogdá nachalsyá dozhd'.
ex.tr: We were sitting in the café when it started to rain.
Suddenly the lights went out.

ex.t: В конце́ концо́в мы нашли́ гости́ницу.
ex.r: V kontsé kontsóv my nashlí gostínitsu.
ex.tr: In the end we found a hotel.

mistakes.wrong: Я пришёл домо́й, сади́лся и открыва́л ноутбу́к.
mistakes.right: Я пришёл домо́й, сел и откры́л ноутбу́к.
mistakes.tr: I came home, sat down and opened my laptop.
mistakes.why: A chain of events, one after another: all perfective.

mistakes.wrong: Когда́ я посмотре́л телеви́зор, позвони́л брат.
mistakes.right: Когда́ я смотре́л телеви́зор, позвони́л брат.
mistakes.tr: While I was watching TV, my brother called.
mistakes.why: The background, “while I was watching”: the imperfective. {{посмотре́л|posmotrél}} would mean you'd finished watching.

practice.t: Когда́ я ___ домо́й, я встре́тил сосе́да.
practice.r: Kogdá ya ___ domóy, ya vstrétil soséda.
practice.tr: When I was walking home, I ran into my neighbor.
He came in, sat down and started talking.

practice.q: {{Мы у́жинали, когда́ позвони́ла ма́ма.|My úzhinali, kogdá pozvoníla máma.}} Which part is the background?
practice.why: {{у́жинали|úzhinali}} is imperfective: what was going on. {{позвони́ла|pozvoníla}} is the event.

practice.q: You're a man, and you're late. Choose your replies.

options: Я е́хал на рабо́ту, и вдруг слома́лась маши́на.
Я пое́хал на рабо́ту, и вдруг лома́лась маши́на.
rs: Ya yékhal na rabótu, i vdrug slomálas' mashína.
Ya poyékhal na rabótu, i vdrug lomálas' mashína.

options: Я позвони́л в серви́с и взял такси́.
Я звони́л в серви́с и брал такси́.
rs: Ya pozvoníl v servís i vzyal taksí.
Ya zvoníl v servís i bral taksí.

practice.tr: First we went for a walk, then we had dinner.

practice.q: Your turn: tell a short story about something that happened to you. Use the imperfective for what was going on and the perfective for what happened.

answers.t: Вчера́ я сиде́ла в кафе́ и пила́ ко́фе. Вдруг ко мне подошёл мужчи́на и сказа́л, что мы вме́сте учи́лись в шко́ле!
answers.r: Vcherá ya sidéla v kafé i pilá kófe. Vdrug ko mne podoshól mushchína i skazál, shto my vméste uchílis' v shkóle!
answers.tr: Yesterday I was sitting in a café, drinking coffee. Suddenly a man came up to me and said we'd been at school together!

answers.t: Мы гуля́ли в па́рке, когда́ начался́ дождь. Мы побежа́ли в кафе́ и там встре́тили друзе́й.

answers.tr: We were walking in the park when it started to rain. We ran to a café and ran into some friends there.

lessons.title: Arrive, leave, go in and out
lessons.summary: Say when someone will arrive or has left, and where people go in, out and across: “He's already left. She'll come at six.”
lessons.topic: Prefixed verbs of motion: {{при-|pri-}}, {{у-|u-}}, {{в-|v-}}, {{вы-|vy-}}, {{пере-|pere-}}, {{за-|za-}}, {{до-|do-}} with {{-йти|-yti}} and {{-е́хать|-ékhat'}}, and their pairs

goal.t: Ива́н уже́ ушёл, но А́нна придёт в шесть.
goal.r: Iván uzhé ushól, no Ánna pridyót v shest'.
goal.tr: Ivan has already left, but Anna will come at six.

dialog.tr: Hello! May I see Ivan Sergeyevich?

dialog.t: Он уже́ ушёл. Он ухо́дит в пять.
dialog.r: On uzhé ushól. On ukhódit v pyat'.
dialog.tr: He's already left. He leaves at five.
And what time does he come in tomorrow?

dialog.t: Обы́чно он прихо́дит в де́вять, но за́втра прие́дет то́лько в оди́ннадцать.
dialog.r: Obýchno on prikhódit v dévyat', no závtra priyédet tól'ko v odínnadtsat'.
dialog.tr: He usually comes in at nine, but tomorrow he won't be here until eleven.
OK, I'll drop by tomorrow.
Goodbye! The exit is on the left.

blocks.p: Add a prefix to {{идти́|idtí}} or {{е́хать|yékhat'}} and the direction becomes precise: {{прийти́|priytí}} “to arrive, to come”, {{уйти́|uytí}} “to leave”, {{войти́|voytí}} “to go in”, {{вы́йти|výyti}} “to go out”. With a prefix, {{идти́|idtí}} becomes {{-йти|-yti}}.

**These are perfective.** {{прийти́|priytí}} is one arrival: {{Я приду́ в шесть.|Ya pridú v shest'.}} “I'll come at six.” {{Он пришёл.|On prishól.}} “He's come, he's here.” Their imperfective partners are made with {{-ходи́ть|-khodít'}} and {{-езжа́ть|-ezzhát'}}: {{приходи́ть|prikhodít'}}, {{уходи́ть|ukhodít'}}, {{приезжа́ть|priyezzhát'}}, {{уезжа́ть|uyezzhát'}}. Use those for habits and for what's going on: {{Он прихо́дит в де́вять.|On prikhódit v dévyat'.}} “He comes in at nine (every day).”

**The forms.** {{прийти́|priytí}}: {{приду́|pridú}}, {{придёшь|pridyósh'}}; past {{пришёл|prishól}}, {{пришла́|prishlá}}, {{пришли́|prishlí}}. {{уйти́|uytí}}: {{уйду́|uydú}}; past {{ушёл|ushól}}, {{ушла́|ushlá}}. {{вы́йти|výyti}}: {{вы́йду|výydu}}; past {{вы́шел|výshel}}, {{вы́шла|výshla}}. {{прие́хать|priyékhat'}} works like {{е́хать|yékhat'}}: {{прие́ду|priyédu}}, {{прие́дешь|priyédesh'}}.

**The prepositions match the prefixes.** {{в|v}} with {{в-|v-}} and {{из|iz}} with {{вы-|vy-}}: {{войти́ в ко́мнату|voytí v kómnatu}}, {{вы́йти из ко́мнаты|výyti iz kómnaty}}. {{к|k}} with {{при-|pri-}} for people: {{прийти́ к дру́гу|priytí k drúgu}}. {{от|ot}} with {{у-|u-}}: {{уйти́ от него́|uytí ot nevó}}. {{до|do}} with {{до-|do-}}: {{дойти́ до метро́|doytí do metró}} “get as far as the subway”.

ex.tr: When will you get here? — On Friday.

ex.t: Он вы́шел из до́ма в семь.

We moved into a new apartment.
Drop by my place after work!

{{вы́йти|výyti}} goes with {{из|iz}} + the genitive.

They moved to a new apartment.

practice.q: You're a tourist in Moscow. Choose your replies.

options: Да, как дойти́ до Кра́сной пло́щади?

answers.tr: I leave for work at seven. Tomorrow some friends are coming over.

lessons.title: Say which one you mean
lessons.summary: Add details about people and things: “the friend who lives in Moscow”, “the book I'm reading”, “the guy she's talking to”.
lessons.topic: {{кото́рый|kotóryy}}: gender and number from the noun, case from its own part of the sentence

goal.t: Как зову́т де́вушку, с кото́рой ты говори́л?
goal.r: Kak zovút dévushku, s kotóroy ty govoríl?
goal.tr: What's the name of the girl you were talking to?

dialog.t: Кто э́то? Де́вушка, кото́рая стои́т у окна́.
dialog.r: Kto éto? Dévushka, kotóraya stoít u okná.
dialog.tr: Who's that? The girl standing by the window.

dialog.t: Э́то Ка́тя. Она́ рабо́тает в фи́рме, кото́рая де́лает и́гры.
dialog.r: Éto Kátya. Oná rabótayet v fírme, kotóraya délayet ígry.
dialog.tr: That's Katya. She works at a company that makes games.

dialog.t: А па́рень, с кото́рым она́ говори́т?
dialog.r: A páren', s kotórym oná govorít?
dialog.tr: And the guy she's talking to?

dialog.t: Э́то её брат. Тот, кото́рого ты ви́дел у меня́ на дне рожде́ния.
dialog.r: Éto yeyó brat. Tot, kotórovo ty vídel u menyá na dne rozhdéniya.
dialog.tr: That's her brother. The one you saw at my birthday party.
Oh, I remember!

blocks.p: {{кото́рый|kotóryy}} “who, which, that” joins a second part to a sentence to say which person or thing you mean. It's an adjective with two masters: its **gender and number** come from the noun it's about, and its **case** comes from its job in its own part of the sentence.

table: {{друг, кото́рый живёт в Москве́|drug, kotóryy zhivyót v Moskvé}}
{{кни́га, кото́рую я чита́ю|kníga, kotóruyu ya chitáyu}}
{{челове́к, с кото́рым я рабо́таю|chelovék, s kotórym ya rabótayu}}
{{фильм, о кото́ром я говори́л|fil'm, o kotórom ya govoríl}}
{{подру́га, кото́рой я звоню́|podrúga, kotóroy ya zvonyú}}
{{друг, у кото́рого есть маши́на|drug, u kotórovo yest' mashína}}

blocks.p: Take {{кни́га, кото́рую я чита́ю|kníga, kotóruyu ya chitáyu}}: {{кни́га|kníga}} is feminine, so {{кото́рая|kotóraya}}; and in its own part it's what I'm reading, the object, so the accusative {{кото́рую|kotóruyu}}. The endings are those of {{но́вый|nóvyy}}. A comma always comes before it. And where English can leave “that” out (“the book I'm reading”), Russian never drops {{кото́рый|kotóryy}}.

ex.t: Э́то мой друг, кото́рый живёт в Москве́.
ex.r: Éto moy drug, kotóryy zhivyót v Moskvé.
ex.tr: This is my friend who lives in Moscow.

ex.t: Где кни́га, кото́рую я тебе́ дал?
ex.r: Gde kníga, kotóruyu ya tebé dal?
ex.tr: Where's the book I gave you?

ex.t: Челове́к, с кото́рым я рабо́таю, — америка́нец.
ex.r: Chelovék, s kotórym ya rabótayu, — amerikánets.
ex.tr: The man I work with is American.

ex.t: Я по́мню фильм, о кото́ром ты говори́шь.
ex.r: Ya pómnyu fil'm, o kotórom ty govorísh'.
ex.tr: I remember the movie you're talking about.

ex.t: У меня́ есть подру́га, кото́рая отли́чно гото́вит.
ex.r: U menyá yest' podrúga, kotóraya otlíchno gotóvit.
ex.tr: I have a friend who's a great cook.

mistakes.tr: The book I'm reading is interesting.
mistakes.why: In its own part, the book is what I'm reading: the accusative {{кото́рую|kotóruyu}}.

mistakes.tr: This is the book I'm reading.
mistakes.why: Russian can't leave out {{кото́рый|kotóryy}} the way English leaves out “that”.

mistakes.tr: This is the girl who lives next door.
mistakes.why: Gender from the noun: {{де́вушка|dévushka}}, so {{кото́рая|kotóraya}}.

practice.tr: This is the movie I told you about.
Where are the letters that came yesterday?
This is the girl I love.

practice.q: In {{друг, у кото́рого есть маши́на|drug, u kotórovo yest' mashína}}, why {{кото́рого|kotórovo}}?
practice.why: Its own job: “at whom” is {{у|u}} + the genitive.

practice.q: A friend is telling you news. Choose your replies.

lines.t: Ты ви́дел Ма́шу? Ту, кото́рая рабо́тает в ба́нке?
lines.r: Ty vídel Máshu? Tu, kotóraya rabótayet v bánke?
lines.tr: Have you seen Masha? The one who works at the bank?

lines.t: Да! А па́рень, с кото́рым она́ живёт, — мой брат!
lines.r: Da! A páren', s kotórym oná zhivyót, — moy brat!
lines.tr: Yes! And the guy she lives with is my brother!

options: Пра́вда? Тот, кото́рый игра́ет на гита́ре?
Пра́вда? Тот, кото́рого игра́ет на гита́ре?
rs: Právda? Tot, kotóryy igráyet na gitáre?
Právda? Tot, kotórovo igráyet na gitáre?

practice.tr: This is the friend I told you about.

practice.q: Your turn: describe two people, places or things with {{кото́рый|kotóryy}}: a friend who…, a book that…, a city where ({{в кото́ром|v kotórom}})…

answers.t: У меня́ есть друг, кото́рый хорошо́ поёт. А кни́га, кото́рую я сейча́с чита́ю, о́чень смешна́я.
answers.r: U menyá yest' drug, kotóryy khoroshó poyót. A kníga, kotóruyu ya seychás chitáyu, óchen' smeshnáya.
answers.tr: I have a friend who sings well. And the book I'm reading now is really funny.

answers.t: Бо́стон — го́род, в кото́ром я роди́лся. Там живу́т лю́ди, кото́рых я о́чень люблю́.
answers.r: Bóston — górod, v kotórom ya rodílsya. Tam zhivút lyúdi, kotórykh ya óchen' lyublyú.
answers.tr: Boston is the city where I was born. People I love very much live there.

lessons.title: Pass on what someone said or asked
lessons.summary: Tell someone what another person said, asked or wants: “She said she'd be late. He asked if you're free.”
lessons.topic: {{сказа́л, что…|skazál, shto…}}; {{спроси́л, где…|sprosíl, gde…}}; {{спроси́л, + ли|sprosíl, + li}}; the tense doesn't change; {{спроси́ть|sprosít'}} and {{попроси́ть|poprosít'}}

goal.t: Ма́ша сказа́ла, что опозда́ет, и спроси́ла, придёшь ли ты.
goal.r: Másha skazála, shto opozdáyet, i sprosíla, pridyósh' li ty.
goal.tr: Masha said she'd be late, and asked whether you're coming.

dialog.tr: Masha called you.
What did she say?

dialog.t: Она́ сказа́ла, что сего́дня не мо́жет прийти́.
dialog.r: Oná skazála, shto sevódnya ne mózhet priytí.
dialog.tr: She said she can't come today.
Why not?

dialog.t: Не зна́ю. Она́ спроси́ла, свобо́дна ли ты в суббо́ту.
dialog.r: Ne znáyu. Oná sprosíla, svobódna li ty v subbótu.
dialog.tr: I don't know. She asked if you're free on Saturday.
Anything else?
And she asked you to call her back.

blocks.p: **Said that.** After {{сказа́ть|skazát'}}, {{ду́мать|dúmat'}}, {{писа́ть|pisát'}} and the like, put {{что|shto}} “that”, then the words as they were said, with only the people changed: {{«Я опозда́ю».|«Ya opozdáyu».}} → {{Ма́ша сказа́ла, что опозда́ет.|Másha skazála, shto opozdáyet.}} Russian doesn't move the tense back as English does (“said she **would** be late”): what was future stays future, what was present stays present. {{что|shto}} can't be left out, and a comma always comes before it.

table: {{Она́ сказа́ла, что опозда́ет.|Oná skazála, shto opozdáyet.}}
{{Он сказа́л, что бо́лен.|On skazál, shto bólen.}}
{{«Мы бы́ли в Москве́».|«My býli v Moskvé».}}
{{Они́ сказа́ли, что бы́ли в Москве́.|Oní skazáli, shto býli v Moskvé.}}

blocks.p: **Asked where, when, what.** A question with a question word keeps it: {{«Где ты живёшь?»|«Gde ty zhivyósh'?»}} → {{Он спроси́л, где я живу́.|On sprosíl, gde ya zhivú.}}

**Asked if.** A yes-or-no question takes {{ли|li}} “whether”, right after the word the question is about, which moves to the front: {{«Ты придёшь?»|«Ty pridyósh'?»}} → {{Она́ спроси́ла, придёшь ли ты.|Oná sprosíla, pridyósh' li ty.}} {{«Ты свобо́дна?»|«Ty svobódna?»}} → {{Он спроси́л, свобо́дна ли ты.|On sprosíl, svobódna li ty.}} Never {{е́сли|yésli}} here: {{е́сли|yésli}} is only for conditions.

**Asked to.** {{спроси́ть|sprosít'}} is to ask a question; {{попроси́ть|poprosít'}} is to ask someone to do something: {{Она́ попроси́ла меня́ позвони́ть.|Oná poprosíla menyá pozvonít'.}} “She asked me to call.”

ex.t: Он сказа́л, что ему́ нра́вится Москва́.
ex.r: On skazál, shto yemú nrávitsa Moskvá.
ex.tr: He said he likes Moscow.
I asked how much the ticket costs.

ex.t: Она́ спроси́ла, говорю́ ли я по-ру́сски.
ex.r: Oná sprosíla, govoryú li ya po-rússki.
ex.tr: She asked if I speak Russian.
Mom asked me to buy bread.
I don't know whether he'll come.

ex.t: Пётр написа́л, что прие́дет в ма́е.
ex.r: Pyotr napisál, shto priyédet v máye.
ex.tr: Pyotr wrote that he'd come in May.

mistakes.why: “Asked if, whether” is {{ли|li}} after the key word, never {{е́сли|yésli}}.
Keep {{что|shto}}: Russian doesn't drop it.

mistakes.tr: I asked him to call me.
mistakes.why: Asking someone to do something is {{попроси́ть|poprosít'}}; {{спроси́ть|sprosít'}} is for questions.

practice.tr: He asked if I'm free tomorrow.
Mom asked me to call Grandma.

practice.q: Anton said {{«Я прие́ду в пя́тницу».|«Ya priyédu v pyátnitsu».}} You pass it on:
options: {{Анто́н сказа́л, что прие́дет в пя́тницу.|Antón skazál, shto priyédet v pyátnitsu.}}
{{Анто́н сказа́л, что прие́хал в пя́тницу.|Antón skazál, shto priyékhal v pyátnitsu.}}
practice.why: The tense doesn't change: future stays future.

practice.q: Your roommate took a call for you. Choose your replies.

lines.why: “What did he say?”: {{Что он сказа́л?|Shto on skazál?}}

lines.t: Он спроси́л, мо́жешь ли ты помо́чь ему́ в суббо́ту.
lines.r: On sprosíl, mózhesh' li ty pomóch' yemú v subbótu.
lines.tr: He asked if you can help him on Saturday.

options: Скажи́ ему́, что я не могу́: мне на́до рабо́тать.
Скажи́ ему́, я не мо́жет: я на́до рабо́тать.
rs: Skazhí yemú, shto ya ne mogú: mne nádo rabótat'.
Skazhí yemú, ya ne mózhet: ya nádo rabótat'.
lines.why: {{что я не могу́|shto ya ne mogú}}, and “I have to”: {{мне на́до|mne nádo}}.

practice.tr: I don't know whether he'll come.

practice.q: Your turn: someone called you today. Pass on what they said ({{сказа́л(а), что…|skazál(a), shto…}}) and what they asked ({{спроси́л(а)…|sprosíl(a)…}}).

answers.t: Мой брат сказа́л, что прие́дет в суббо́ту, и спроси́л, бу́дем ли мы до́ма.
answers.r: Moy brat skazál, shto priyédet v subbótu, i sprosíl, búdem li my dóma.
answers.tr: My brother said he's coming on Saturday, and asked whether we'll be home.

answers.t: Подру́га сказа́ла, что у неё но́вая рабо́та, и спроси́ла, где мы встре́тимся.
answers.r: Podrúga skazála, shto u neyó nóvaya rabóta, i sprosíla, gde my vstrétimsya.
answers.tr: My friend said she has a new job, and asked where we're meeting.

lessons.title: Say what for, and what you want others to do
lessons.summary: Explain your purpose, and say what you want other people to do: “I'm learning Russian to read Tolstoy.” “I want you to come.”
lessons.topic: {{что́бы|shtóby}} + infinitive (the same person) and {{что́бы|shtóby}} + past (another person): {{Я хочу́, что́бы ты пришёл.|Ya khochú, shtóby ty prishól.}}

goal.t: Я учу́ ру́сский, что́бы чита́ть Толсто́го в оригина́ле.
goal.r: Ya uchú rússkiy, shtóby chitát' Tolstóvo v originále.
goal.tr: I'm learning Russian to read Tolstoy in the original.

dialog.tr: Why are you getting up so early?

dialog.t: Что́бы успе́ть в спортза́л пе́ред рабо́той.
dialog.r: Shtóby uspét' v sportzál péred rabótoy.
dialog.tr: To make it to the gym before work.

dialog.t: Молоде́ц. А я хочу́, что́бы ты ча́ще звони́л ба́бушке.
dialog.r: Molodéts. A ya khochú, shtóby ty cháshche zvoníl bábushke.
dialog.tr: Good for you. And I want you to call Grandma more often.
OK, I'll call her today.

dialog.t: И скажи́ ей, что́бы она́ не волнова́лась.
dialog.r: I skazhí yey, shtóby oná ne volnoválas'.
dialog.tr: And tell her not to worry.

blocks.p: **In order to.** {{что́бы|shtóby}} + an infinitive says what for, when it's the same person: {{Я учу́ ру́сский, что́бы чита́ть Толсто́го.|Ya uchú rússkiy, shtóby chitát' Tolstóvo.}} “I'm learning Russian to read Tolstoy.” It's the answer to {{Заче́м?|Zachém?}} “What for?” from lesson 38.

**I want you to…** When someone else is to do it, Russian can't say “I want you to come” word for word. It says “I want that you came”: {{что́бы|shtóby}} + the **past** tense, whatever the time: {{Я хочу́, что́бы ты пришёл.|Ya khochú, shtóby ty prishól.}} “I want you to come.” This past doesn't mean the past: it's simply the form {{что́бы|shtóby}} takes.

table: {{Я хочу́ прийти́.|Ya khochú priytí.}} I want to come.
{{Я хочу́, что́бы ты пришёл.|Ya khochú, shtóby ty prishól.}} I want you to come.
{{Я рабо́таю, что́бы жить.|Ya rabótayu, shtóby zhit'.}} I work to live.
{{Я рабо́таю, что́бы де́ти учи́лись.|Ya rabótayu, shtóby déti uchílis'.}} I work so my kids can study.
{{Скажи́ ему́, что́бы он позвони́л.|Skazhí yemú, shtóby on pozvoníl.}} Tell him to call.

blocks.p: **Telling and asking.** After {{сказа́ть|skazát'}} and {{попроси́ть|poprosít'}}, {{что́бы|shtóby}} + the past passes on a request: {{Он сказа́л, что́бы ты подожда́л.|On skazál, shtóby ty podozhdál.}} “He said for you to wait.” Compare {{Он сказа́л, что ты подожда́л.|On skazál, shto ty podozhdál.}} “He said that you waited.” One little {{-бы|-by}} changes everything.

ex.tr: I came to help.

ex.t: Мы откры́ли окно́, что́бы бы́ло не так жа́рко.
ex.r: My otkrýli oknó, shtóby býlo ne tak zhárko.
ex.tr: We opened the window so it wouldn't be so hot.

ex.t: Я хочу́, что́бы ты был сча́стлив.
ex.r: Ya khochú, shtóby ty byl shchástliv.
ex.tr: I want you to be happy.

ex.t: Ма́ма хо́чет, что́бы я стал врачо́м.
ex.r: Máma khóchet, shtóby ya stal vrachóm.
ex.tr: Mom wants me to become a doctor.

ex.t: Попроси́ его́, что́бы он говори́л ме́дленнее.
ex.r: Poprosí yevó, shtóby on govoríl médlenneye.
ex.tr: Ask him to speak more slowly.
What do you need to get a visa?

mistakes.why: “I want you to…” is {{хочу́, что́бы|khochú, shtóby}} + the past.
After {{что́бы|shtóby}} with another person: the past form.

mistakes.wrong: Я учу́ ру́сский для чита́ть кни́ги.
mistakes.right: Я учу́ ру́сский, что́бы чита́ть кни́ги.
mistakes.tr: I'm learning Russian to read books.
mistakes.why: “To, in order to” before a verb is {{что́бы|shtóby}}; {{для|dlya}} goes before a noun.

practice.t: Я хочу́, что́бы ты ___ ко мне.
practice.r: Ya khochú, shtóby ty ___ ko mne.
practice.tr: I want you to come to my place.
He works to buy a house.

practice.q: {{Скажи́ ему́, что́бы он позвони́л|Skazhí yemú, shtóby on pozvoníl}} means…
practice.why: {{что́бы|shtóby}} + the past passes on a request. “That he called” would be {{что он позвони́л|shto on pozvoníl}}.

practice.q: A friend asks why you're learning Russian. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: What are you learning Russian for?

options: Потому́ что говори́ть с ру́сскими друзья́ми.
rs: Potomú shto govorít' s rússkimi druz'yámi.

lines.r: A shto ty khóchesh', shtóby ya sdélal?
lines.tr: And what do you want me to do?

options: Я хочу́, что́бы ты говори́л со мной то́лько по-ру́сски!
Я хочу́, что́бы ты говори́шь со мной то́лько по-ру́сски!
rs: Ya khochú, shtóby ty govoríl so mnoy tól'ko po-rússki!
Ya khochú, shtóby ty govorísh' so mnoy tól'ko po-rússki!

practice.tr: Ask him to speak more slowly.

practice.q: Say: “I want you to be happy.”
practice.answer: Я хочу́, что́бы ты был сча́стлив.

practice.q: Your turn: why are you learning Russian ({{что́бы|shtóby}} + infinitive), and what do you want someone else to do ({{хочу́, что́бы|khochú, shtóby}} + past)?

answers.t: Я учу́ ру́сский, что́бы понима́ть ру́сские фи́льмы. И я хочу́, что́бы мой брат то́же его́ учи́л.

answers.t: Я учу́ ру́сский, что́бы рабо́тать в Москве́. Я хочу́, что́бы моя́ семья́ прие́хала ко мне.
answers.r: Ya uchú rússkiy, shtóby rabótat' v Moskvé. Ya khochú, shtóby moyá sem'yá priyékhala ko mne.

lessons.title: Give your opinion, agree and disagree
lessons.summary: Say what you think, agree, or politely disagree: “In my opinion, it's a great idea.” “I agree with you.” “I'm not sure.”
lessons.topic: {{по-мо́ему|po-móyemu}}, {{мне ка́жется|mne kázhetsa}}, {{я счита́ю|ya shchitáyu}}, {{я ду́маю, что…|ya dúmayu, shto…}}; {{я согла́сен|ya soglásen}} / {{согла́сна с|soglásna s}} + instrumental

goal.t: По-мо́ему, э́то отли́чная иде́я. Я с тобо́й согла́сен.
goal.r: Po-móyemu, éto otlíchnaya idéya. Ya s tobóy soglásen.
goal.tr: I think it's a great idea. I agree with you.

dialog.t: Как ты счита́ешь, где лу́чше жить: в го́роде и́ли в дере́вне?
dialog.r: Kak ty shchitáyesh', gde lúchshe zhit': v górode íli v derévne?
dialog.tr: What do you think: is it better to live in the city or in the country?

dialog.t: Мне ка́жется, в го́роде. Там бо́льше рабо́ты, и интере́снее.
dialog.r: Mne kázhetsa, v górode. Tam ból'she rabóty, i interésneye.
dialog.tr: I think in the city. There's more work there, and it's more interesting.

dialog.t: Я не согла́сна. В дере́вне споко́йнее, и во́здух чи́ще.
dialog.r: Ya ne soglásna. V derévne spokóyneye, i vózdukh chíshche.
dialog.tr: I disagree. It's calmer in the country, and the air is cleaner.

dialog.t: Мо́жет быть, ты права́. Но там ску́чно!
dialog.r: Mózhet byt', ty pravá. No tam skúshno!
dialog.tr: Maybe you're right. But it's boring there!
Well, it's a matter of taste.

blocks.p: **Saying what you think.** {{По-мо́ему…|Po-móyemu…}} “In my opinion…” (and {{по-тво́ему|po-tvóyemu}}, {{по-ва́шему|po-váshemu}} “in your opinion”). {{Мне ка́жется, (что)…|Mne kázhetsa, (shto)…}} “It seems to me…”: soft, and very common. {{Я ду́маю, что…|Ya dúmayu, shto…}} “I think that…”. {{Я счита́ю, что…|Ya shchitáyu, shto…}} “I believe, I'm convinced that…”: firmer. To ask: {{Как ты ду́маешь?|Kak ty dúmayesh'?}}, {{Как ты счита́ешь?|Kak ty shchitáyesh'?}}, {{Что ты ду́маешь о…?|Shto ty dúmayesh' o…?}}

**Agreeing.** {{согла́сен|soglásen}} “in agreement” is a short adjective like {{рад|rad}}: {{я согла́сен|ya soglásen}} (a man), {{я согла́сна|ya soglásna}} (a woman), {{мы согла́сны|my soglásny}}. With whom: {{с|s}} + the instrumental, {{Я с тобо́й согла́сна.|Ya s tobóy soglásna.}} “I agree with you.” And from lesson 36: {{Ты прав|Ty prav}}, {{Ты права́|Ty pravá}} “You're right”.

table: {{Я не согла́сен.|Ya ne soglásen.}} / {{Я не согла́сна.|Ya ne soglásna.}}
{{Я не уве́рен.|Ya ne uvéren.}} / {{Я не уве́рена.|Ya ne uvérena.}}

blocks.p: **Softening.** {{наве́рное|navérnoye}} “probably”, {{мо́жет быть|mózhet byt'}} “maybe”, {{коне́чно|konéshno}} “of course”, {{че́стно говоря́|chéstno govoryá}} “to be honest”. To disagree politely, start by agreeing: {{Да, но…|Da, no…}}, or weigh both sides: {{С одно́й стороны́…, с друго́й стороны́…|S odnóy storoný…, s drugóy storoný…}} “On the one hand…, on the other…”.

ex.tr: I think he's right.
Do you think she'll come?
I believe that's wrong.

ex.t: Че́стно говоря́, мне не понра́вился фильм.
ex.r: Chéstno govoryá, mne ne ponrávilsya fil'm.
ex.tr: To be honest, I didn't like the movie.

ex.t: С одно́й стороны́, э́то до́рого, с друго́й — о́чень удо́бно.
ex.r: S odnóy storoný, éto dórogo, s drugóy — óchen' udóbno.
ex.tr: On the one hand it's expensive, on the other it's very convenient.
I completely agree with you.

mistakes.why: Agree with someone: {{с|s}} + the instrumental.

mistakes.wrong: Как ты ду́маешь об э́том фи́льме?
mistakes.right: Что ты ду́маешь об э́том фи́льме?
mistakes.tr: What do you think of this movie?
mistakes.why: “What do you think of…?” is {{Что ты ду́маешь о…?|Shto ty dúmayesh' o…?}}. {{Как|Kak}} goes alone: {{Как ты ду́маешь?|Kak ty dúmayesh'?}}
A woman says {{согла́сна|soglásna}}.

practice.tr: I agree with you. (a woman speaking)
What do you think of this book?
practice.why: {{Что ты ду́маешь о…?|Shto ty dúmayesh' o…?}}

options: {{Мне ка́жется, э́то не о́чень хоро́шая иде́я.|Mne kázhetsa, éto ne óchen' khoróshaya idéya.}}
{{Я счита́ю, что э́то плоха́я иде́я.|Ya shchitáyu, shto éto plokháya idéya.}}
practice.why: {{Мне ка́жется|Mne kázhetsa}} and {{не о́чень хоро́шая|ne óchen' khoróshaya}} both soften it.

practice.q: A colleague asks your opinion. Choose your replies.

lines.t: Как вы счита́ете, где лу́чше рабо́тать: до́ма и́ли в о́фисе?
lines.r: Kak vy shchitáyete, gde lúchshe rabótat': dóma íli v ófise?
lines.tr: What do you think: is it better to work from home or at the office?

options: По-мо́ему, до́ма лу́чше: споко́йнее, и не на́до е́хать на рабо́ту.
По-мо́ему, до́ма бо́лее хоро́ший: споко́йный, и не на́до е́хать на рабо́ту.

Po-móyemu, dóma bóleye khoróshiy: spokóynyy, i ne nádo yékhat' na rabótu.
